questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a CT of his chest for a cough, which incidentally shows a 14 mm nodule in the left thyroid lobe. He has no neck symptoms, weight loss or voice change. There are no palpable lymph nodes. His TSH is 1.8 mU/L (0.4–4.0).
questions.q: Which is the most likely nature of the nodule?
questions.e: Most thyroid nodules, especially incidental ones without red flags, are benign; absence of red flags favours a benign nodule.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: no neck symptoms, weight loss or voice change
steps.x: An asymptomatic incidental nodule with no red flags.

elim: Rapid goitre growth, usually on a background of Hashimoto's.
Rare; family history or MEN2 features would be expected.
Rare in the thyroid; no lung mass was found.

steps.x: **B. Benign nodule.** Most nodules are benign, particularly without red flags.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has noticed a lump in her neck. As a child she had mantle radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. Her mother has hypertension and her father has type 2 diabetes. She smokes 5 cigarettes a day. Ultrasound shows a solitary 2 cm thyroid nodule.
questions.q: Which feature in her history most increases her risk of thyroid cancer?
questions.e: Prior radiation exposure is the most important risk factor for thyroid malignancy (with family history of thyroid cancer).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Childhood radiation to the neck.

elim: Papillary can occur in young adults, but age is not the main risk factor.
Nodules and cancer are more common in women, but radiation is the strongest risk.
Not a thyroid cancer risk factor.
Not a recognised thyroid cancer risk factor.

steps.x: **D. Prior neck radiotherapy.** Thyroid nodule + previous radiation = higher cancer risk.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has a 2 cm lump to the right of the midline in the lower neck. It moves up when she swallows but does not move when she sticks out her tongue. It is not tender. Her TSH is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Thyroid nodules move on swallowing (attached to the larynx by pretracheal fascia) but not on tongue protrusion; thyroglossal cysts are midline and rise with tongue protrusion.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: to the right of the midline
does not move when she sticks out her tongue
steps.x: Moves with swallowing only, off the midline.

elim: Anterior to sternocleidomastoid at the angle of the jaw, does not move on swallowing.
Soft, superficial, does not move with swallowing.
Does not move on swallowing and is often tender.
The key differential: midline and rises with tongue protrusion.

steps.x: **E. Thyroid nodule.** Swallow yes, tongue no = thyroid; swallow and tongue = thyroglossal cyst.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has a 2 cm painless thyroid nodule and a firm 1.5 cm node in the right side of her neck. She is otherwise well. Her TSH is normal. FNA of the nodule is malignant.
questions.q: Which is the most likely type of thyroid cancer?
questions.e: Papillary carcinoma is the commonest type (about 60%), typically a solitary nodule in women aged 30 to 40 with early spread to cervical lymph nodes.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: FNA of the nodule is malignant
steps.x: Young woman, solitary nodule, early nodal spread.

elim: Presents later and spreads in the blood, not early to nodes.
Rapid diffuse goitre, often with Hashimoto's.
Rare; raised calcitonin and MEN2 history.

steps.x: **E. Papillary carcinoma.** Young woman + nodule + cervical node = papillary.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has a 4 cm thyroid nodule present for some years. She has developed a dry cough. Chest X-ray shows several rounded lesions in both lungs. Neck ultrasound shows no enlarged lymph nodes. Calcitonin is normal.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Multiple rounded lung lesions: cannonball metastases.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Follicular carcinoma presents later, in women, and spreads haematogenously to lung and bone rather than lymph nodes.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: several rounded lesions in both lungs
steps.x: Blood-borne lung metastases with no nodal spread.

elim: Rapid local growth and compression, not a long-standing nodule.
Benign; does not cause lung metastases.
Spreads mainly to cervical lymph nodes first.

steps.x: **B. Follicular carcinoma.** Follicular = haematogenous to lung and bone.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has a hard thyroid nodule. He has episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations, with a BP of 196/112 mmHg during one. His serum calcitonin is markedly raised and 24-hour urinary metanephrines are high.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying syndrome?
questions.e: Medullary thyroid carcinoma (raised calcitonin, from C cells) with a phaeochromocytoma is MEN type 2.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Medullary carcinoma plus phaeochromocytoma.

elim: Parathyroid, pituitary and pancreas; not medullary thyroid cancer.
Phaeochromocytoma can occur, but not medullary thyroid cancer.

steps.x: **B. MEN type 2.** Calcitonin + phaeochromocytoma = medullary carcinoma in MEN2.

questions.stem: An 84 year old man has a neck mass that has doubled in size in 3 weeks. He now has noisy breathing, difficulty swallowing and a hoarse voice. The mass is hard and fixed and there are large cervical lymph nodes. His SpO2 is 94% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Anaplastic carcinoma is the rarest and most aggressive type, presenting late in the elderly with rapid growth, compressive symptoms and cervical lymphadenopathy.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Elderly, rapid growth, compression, fixed mass.

elim: Sudden painful swelling, not a hard fixed mass with nodes.

steps.x: **A. Anaplastic carcinoma.** Elderly + rapid growth + compression = anaplastic.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman is seen in a thyroid clinic with a 3 cm thyroid nodule. Her TSH is normal. Several features are recorded on examination and history.
questions.q: Which feature most strongly suggests malignancy?
o: Fixed irregular mass with cervical lymphadenopathy
questions.e: Red flags for malignancy include a fixed irregular mass, lymphadenopathy, weight loss, dysphagia, hoarseness and rapid growth.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Look for the red flag among reassuring features.
**A. Fixed irregular mass with cervical lymphadenopathy.** Fixed, irregular, nodes, rapid growth, hoarseness = red flags.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has a known 2 cm benign thyroid nodule. She woke this morning with sudden pain in the front of her neck and the lump is now larger and tender. She has no fever. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and TSH is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Pain is rare with thyroid nodules; sudden painful enlargement of a known benign nodule is usually haemorrhage into it.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Abrupt painful enlargement without fever or thyrotoxicosis.

elim: Over weeks, in the elderly, with a hard fixed mass.
Follows a viral illness, with fever and thyrotoxicosis.

steps.x: **B. Haemorrhage into the nodule.** Nodules are rarely painful; sudden pain = bleed into a nodule.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has weight loss, palpitations and tremor. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm. She has a single 3 cm thyroid nodule and no eye signs. TSH is undetectable and free T4 raised. Radionuclide scan shows uptake only in the nodule, with the rest of the gland suppressed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A single 'hot' nodule with suppression of the rest of the gland is a benign autonomously functioning (toxic) adenoma.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Hyperthyroid with one hot nodule.

elim: Diffuse uptake, often with eye signs.
Cold on scanning and usually euthyroid.

steps.x: **D. Toxic adenoma.** Single hot nodule = toxic adenoma (benign).

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman had a total thyroidectomy 2 days ago. Since waking from the anaesthetic her voice has been weak and breathy, and she coughs when drinking water. Her calcium is 2.31 mmol/L (2.2–2.6) and she has no neck swelling.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Recurrent laryngeal nerve damage during thyroidectomy causes hoarseness and a weak voice; the nerve runs close to the inferior thyroid artery.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: voice has been weak and breathy
steps.x: Voice change from the moment of surgery, normal calcium, no swelling.

elim: Perioral tingling and cramps; her calcium is normal.
Facial swelling and distended neck veins.
Neck swelling at 4 to 6 hours, with stridor.

steps.x: **C. Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.** Post-thyroidectomy hoarseness = recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman had a hemithyroidectomy 5 hours ago. A nurse calls because she has a tense swelling under the wound, is anxious and has noisy breathing. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and SpO2 92% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Neck swelling 4 to 6 hours after thyroid surgery with airway compromise is a wound haematoma: remove the sutures immediately to decompress it.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Swelling under the wound and stridor in the first hours.

elim: Rash, wheeze and hypotension, not a localised wound swelling.
Stridor at extubation, no wound swelling, and unlikely after a hemithyroidectomy.
Usually after 24 hours, without neck swelling.

steps.x: **E. Wound haematoma.** Swelling + stridor at 4 to 6 hours = haematoma: open the wound.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has a hemithyroidectomy for a 2.5 cm nodule. Histology shows papillary structures with cells that have clear, empty-looking nuclei and scattered laminated calcified bodies.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: 'Orphan Annie eye' nuclei and psammoma bodies are characteristic of papillary carcinoma.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Orphan Annie eye nuclei and psammoma bodies.

elim: Defined by capsular and vascular invasion.

steps.x: **E. Papillary carcinoma.** Orphan Annie + psammoma = papillary.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman has a hard neck lump that she first noticed a month ago and that has grown quickly. She has lost 6 kg and finds solid food sticks. Her daughter says her voice has become croaky. Ultrasound shows an infiltrative mass invading the trachea.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Anaplastic carcinoma is the most aggressive thyroid cancer, in elderly patients with rapid growth and local invasion causing compressive symptoms.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Elderly, rapid, locally invasive.
**A. Anaplastic carcinoma.** Anaplastic: rarest, most aggressive, elderly.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman noticed a lump in her neck while putting on a necklace. Examination shows a 2 cm smooth nodule in the right thyroid lobe that moves on swallowing. She has no other symptoms. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Every thyroid nodule starts with thyroid function tests (TSH first), alongside ultrasound; a low TSH changes the pathway to a radionuclide scan.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
A new nodule: first know the thyroid status.

elim: Not first-line; used for staging or retrosternal extension.
For suspected medullary cancer or surveillance.

steps.x: **E. Thyroid function tests (TSH).** Thyroid nodule: TSH first.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has a 2 cm thyroid nodule. His TSH is normal. Neck ultrasound is performed to decide whether fine-needle aspiration is needed.
questions.q: Which ultrasound feature most suggests malignancy?
questions.e: Ultrasound stratifies risk: hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications and irregular margins are suspicious and prompt FNA.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.

clues: decide whether fine-needle aspiration is needed
steps.x: Which feature is a suspicious one?
**C. Microcalcifications within a hypoechoic nodule.** Suspicious: hypoechoic, microcalcifications, irregular margins.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a hard 3 cm thyroid nodule. His TSH is 1.2 mU/L. Ultrasound shows a hypoechoic nodule with irregular margins. He has no lymphadenopathy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: FNA is the key diagnostic test for a large or ultrasound-suspicious nodule; cytology is reported as benign, indeterminate or malignant.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
Normal TSH, suspicious ultrasound.

elim: Delays diagnosis of a suspicious nodule.
A marker for follow-up after thyroidectomy, not diagnosis.

steps.x: **E. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration.** Suspicious ultrasound = FNA.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman has a 2.5 cm thyroid nodule. FNA cytology is reported as indeterminate, showing a follicular lesion. Her TSH is normal and ultrasound shows no lymphadenopathy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Follicular carcinoma differs from adenoma only by capsular and vascular invasion, which needs histology, not FNA; so indeterminate follicular cytology needs a diagnostic hemithyroidectomy.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
FNA cannot tell follicular adenoma from carcinoma.

elim: Used after thyroidectomy for cancer, not for an undiagnosed nodule.

steps.x: **A. Diagnostic hemithyroidectomy.** Indeterminate follicular FNA = diagnostic lobectomy for histology.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with mild thyrotoxicosis and a low TSH has a radionuclide thyroid scan of a 2.5 cm nodule. The nodule shows reduced uptake compared with the rest of the gland, which takes up tracer normally.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Repeat radionuclide scan in a year
questions.e: A 'cold' nodule carries a higher risk of malignancy than a 'hot' one, so it needs ultrasound-guided FNA.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.

clues: reduced uptake compared with the rest of the gland
steps.x: A cold nodule on scanning.

elim: Does not give a tissue diagnosis.

steps.x: **B. Fine-needle aspiration of the nodule.** Hot = benign autonomous; cold = needs FNA.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has a 2 cm thyroid nodule. His TSH is 0.05 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is at the upper limit of normal. A radionuclide scan shows intense uptake in the nodule and suppression of the rest of the gland.
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation?
questions.e: A 'hot' nodule suggests benign autonomous function, so FNA is not usually needed.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
Low TSH and a hot nodule.

elim: Arises from C cells, which do not take up tracer.

steps.x: **A. Benign autonomously functioning nodule.** Hot nodule = benign autonomous function.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman had a total thyroidectomy for medullary thyroid carcinoma 2 months ago. She feels well. Her team plans tumour marker surveillance to detect recurrence.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate tumour marker?
questions.e: Medullary carcinoma arises from C cells, which secrete calcitonin, so serum calcitonin is used for diagnosis and surveillance.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
Match the marker to the cell of origin.

elim: Hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumours.
For papillary and follicular cancer after thyroidectomy.

steps.x: **C. Serum calcitonin.** Medullary = calcitonin; papillary/follicular = thyroglobulin.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man has had a total thyroidectomy for medullary thyroid carcinoma. His post-operative serum calcitonin is detectable but falling. He asks how often it will be checked.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate surveillance schedule?
o: Every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months for 3 years, then annually
questions.e: Calcitonin surveillance for medullary cancer is every 3 months for 2 years, then 6-monthly for 3 years, then annually once undetectable.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
Structured, front-loaded surveillance.

elim: Too infrequent to detect early recurrence.
One test cannot exclude later recurrence.

steps.x: **A. Every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months for 3 years, then annually.** Calcitonin: 3-monthly for 2 years, 6-monthly for 3 years, then yearly.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant has a 15 mm thyroid nodule. Her TSH is normal. Ultrasound features are benign and she has no red flags. She is anxious about her baby.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Urgent thyroidectomy in the second trimester
questions.e: A benign-appearing nodule in pregnancy is managed with reassurance and monitoring, reassessing after delivery.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
Benign nodule; pregnancy only changes the timing.

elim: For thyrotoxic nodules or cancer, not a benign euthyroid nodule.
Not indicated for a benign nodule.

steps.x: **B. Reassure and monitor, reassessing postpartum.** Benign nodule in pregnancy: reassure, review postpartum.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has a toxic adenoma: a single hot nodule on scan with a suppressed TSH. She has palpitations and weight loss. She wants a definitive treatment but plans to start a family within 6 months and wants to avoid radiation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Surgical removal of the affected lobe (hemithyroidectomy)
questions.e: A thyrotoxic nodule is treated by managing the hyperthyroidism, with radioiodine or surgery; she wants to avoid radiation before pregnancy, so surgery.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
Definitive treatment without radiation.

elim: An option normally, but pregnancy must be avoided for months afterwards.
Cancer surgery; overtreatment for a benign adenoma.

steps.x: **D. Surgical removal of the affected lobe (hemithyroidectomy).** Toxic nodule: radioiodine or surgery.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman had a diagnostic hemithyroidectomy for an indeterminate nodule. Histology shows a 4.5 cm follicular carcinoma with capsular and vascular invasion. Staging CT shows no distant metastases.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Completion thyroidectomy followed by radioactive iodine
questions.e: Malignant nodules are treated with total (or partial) thyroidectomy, with radioactive iodine as secondary treatment to ablate remnant tissue.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
A large, invasive differentiated cancer after a lobectomy.

elim: Reserved for unresectable or anaplastic disease.
Inadequate for a 4.5 cm invasive cancer.

steps.x: **A. Completion thyroidectomy followed by radioactive iodine.** Differentiated thyroid cancer = thyroidectomy + radioiodine.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman develops tingling around her lips and cramps in her hands 20 hours after a total thyroidectomy. Tapping in front of her ear makes her face twitch. Her adjusted calcium is 1.71 mmol/L (2.2–2.6). Her ECG shows a prolonged QT interval.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Severe symptomatic post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia (perioral paraesthesia, Chvostek's sign, long QT) from parathyroid injury needs IV calcium gluconate.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
Severe, symptomatic hypocalcaemia with ECG change.

elim: For mild hypocalcaemia; too slow here.
Needed long term, but does not treat calcium.
No neck swelling; the problem is calcium.

steps.x: **A. IV calcium gluconate.** Severe post-op hypocalcaemia = IV calcium gluconate.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man had a total thyroidectomy 4 hours ago. He has a rapidly enlarging neck swelling, stridor and is struggling to breathe. His SpO2 is 89% on 15 L oxygen and pulse rate 124 bpm. The surgical team is 20 minutes away.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Nebulised adrenaline and wait for the surgeon
Open the wound and remove the sutures at the bedside
questions.e: A post-thyroidectomy wound haematoma compressing the airway is managed immediately by opening the wound and removing the sutures to evacuate the clot.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
Airway compression from a haematoma; time matters.
**D. Open the wound and remove the sutures at the bedside.** Neck haematoma with stridor: open the wound at the bedside, now.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has medullary thyroid carcinoma confirmed on FNA with a raised calcitonin. A phaeochromocytoma has been excluded. Staging shows disease confined to the neck.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Malignant nodules are treated with thyroidectomy. Medullary cancer arises from C cells, which do not take up iodine, so radioactive iodine is not effective.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
Medullary cancer, after excluding phaeochromocytoma.

elim: Does not treat C cell tumours.
C cells do not concentrate iodine.

steps.x: **E. Total thyroidectomy.** Medullary = total thyroidectomy (radioiodine does not work).

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has a 12 mm thyroid nodule found on a carotid scan. His TSH is normal. Ultrasound shows a spongiform nodule with benign features and FNA was not indicated. He has no red flags.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Benign nodules are managed with reassurance and monitoring; only a small minority of nodules are malignant.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
A low-risk incidental nodule.

elim: Surgery for a benign, asymptomatic nodule is overtreatment.
He is euthyroid; suppression therapy is not recommended.

steps.x: **C. Reassurance with follow-up.** Benign nodule = reassure and monitor.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with a 2 cm thyroid nodule asks why her surgeon says it is unlikely to be cancer. Her FNA is reported as benign, showing abundant colloid and benign follicular cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying pathology of most thyroid nodules?
questions.e: Most nodules arise from benign hyperplastic or colloid change, or true adenomas; only a small minority are malignant.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.

clues: abundant colloid and benign follicular cells
steps.x: Colloid on cytology.

elim: Rare, often on a background of Hashimoto's.

steps.x: **A. Benign hyperplastic or colloid change.** Most nodules = benign colloid/hyperplastic change or adenoma.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman had a hemithyroidectomy for a follicular lesion. The pathologist reports tumour cells breaching the capsule and invading blood vessels. A bone scan later shows a lesion in her pelvis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Capsular and vascular invasion distinguish follicular carcinoma from adenoma and explain its haematogenous spread to bone and lung.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.

clues: breaching the capsule and invading blood vessels
steps.x: Invasion on histology and a blood-borne bone metastasis.

elim: Orphan Annie nuclei; spreads to lymph nodes.

steps.x: **C. Follicular carcinoma.** Capsular + vascular invasion = follicular carcinoma: blood-borne spread.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has a thyroid nodule and a raised serum calcitonin. FNA shows spindle-shaped cells in an amyloid stroma. His brother had the same tumour.
questions.q: From which cells does this tumour most likely arise?
o: Squamous cells of the thyroglossal duct
questions.e: Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, derived from the neural crest, which secrete calcitonin.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.
Calcitonin-secreting tumour.

elim: Give papillary, follicular and anaplastic cancers.

steps.x: **C. Neural crest-derived parafollicular C cells.** Medullary = C cells (neural crest) = calcitonin.

questions.stem: A surgeon is ligating vessels to the lower pole of the thyroid during a total thyroidectomy. She takes care to identify a nerve closely related to one artery, because injury would affect the patient's voice.
questions.q: Which artery is the recurrent laryngeal nerve most closely related to?
questions.e: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close to the inferior thyroid artery and is vulnerable during surgery (and to malignant infiltration), causing hoarseness.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.
The nerve at risk at the lower pole.

elim: Not related to the thyroid lower pole.
Runs with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
Posterior, not in the operative field.

steps.x: **B. Inferior thyroid artery.** Recurrent laryngeal nerve: next to the inferior thyroid artery.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has papillary thyroid carcinoma. Staging shows enlarged nodes in the central and lateral neck but no distant disease. She asks why the cancer is in her neck glands.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route of spread?
questions.e: Papillary carcinoma spreads via lymphatics, giving early cervical node metastases; follicular spreads haematogenously.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.

clues: enlarged nodes in the central and lateral neck
steps.x: Nodal spread in papillary cancer.

elim: Across body cavities, e.g. ovarian cancer.

steps.x: **C. Lymphatic spread.** Papillary = lymphatic; follicular = blood.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman had a total thyroidectomy for papillary carcinoma 3 months ago. She still needs calcium and alfacalcidol tablets. Her PTH is undetectable.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her ongoing need for calcium?
o: Permanent injury or devascularisation of the parathyroid glands
questions.e: Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia comes from injury to or devascularisation of the adjacent parathyroid glands; undetectable PTH at 3 months suggests permanent hypoparathyroidism.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.
Low calcium with absent PTH after neck surgery.

elim: Calcitonin has minimal effect on calcium in humans.
After parathyroidectomy, with high PTH beforehand.
Replaced with levothyroxine; does not cause hypocalcaemia.
PTH would be high, not undetectable.

steps.x: **D. Permanent injury or devascularisation of the parathyroid glands.** Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia = parathyroid damage.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman was diagnosed with papillary thyroid carcinoma with nodal spread 6 years ago but declined surgery. She now has a cough and breathlessness on exertion. Her SpO2 is 95% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Multiple small nodules in both lungs: metastases.

questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her chest X-ray?
questions.e: Untreated papillary carcinoma spreads to lymph nodes and then the lungs, giving multiple small pulmonary nodules.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: papillary thyroid carcinoma with nodal spread
steps.x: Untreated thyroid cancer, now lung lesions.

elim: Would be focal consolidation with fever.
Usually a single mass; she has a known untreated cancer.
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, not multiple nodules.
Upper zone cavitation with systemic symptoms.

steps.x: **A. Lung metastases from papillary carcinoma.** Papillary spreads to nodes then lungs; follicular to bone and lung.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has had a total thyroidectomy for a 3 cm papillary carcinoma with central neck nodes. She has recovered well and her calcium is normal. Her team discuss treatment to destroy any remaining thyroid tissue.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.e: Malignant nodules are treated with thyroidectomy, with radioactive iodine as secondary treatment to ablate remnant thyroid and microscopic disease in differentiated cancers.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
Differentiated cancer after surgery, needing remnant ablation.

elim: The gland has already been removed.

steps.x: **D. Radioactive iodine.** Papillary/follicular: surgery, then radioiodine.
